rulings.currentText: | `relay_pull_in_v` / `drop_out_v` | 7.5 / 3.0 (or MV601-REF-A's 6.5 / 2.5 — pick one and use it everywhere) |
rulings.ruling: Delete the 7.5 / 3.0 option. The row must read `relay_pull_in_v` / `drop_out_v` = 6.5 / 2.5, matching MV601-REF-A, and carry the note: 7.5 V is refuted by this file's own AT-01 — SDC's simplest published latch would not pull in. Replace the parenthetical '(pick one and use it everywhere)' with 'MV601-REF-A is the single source of these two constants; §9.3 must not restate them at a different value.'
rulings.evidence: Internal, and decisive. §8.2 AT-01: the Book I Experiment 9 latch drives the coil through its own indicator lamp, giving V_coil = 6.92 V, and the row itself says 'Fails first if pull-in is raised above ~6.9 V'. 6.92 V < 7.5 V, so under §9.3's shipped default the canonical self-holding relay of BK1 printed p.17 (program 1F/1-, 1C/1X, 1Y/2Y, 2Y/2+, 2Z/1L, 1K/1C — re-read on the page image) never latches. rulings.tag_change: none (both figures already [unverified]); this is a contradiction, not a tag error

rulings.currentText: **Armature as a continuous travel scalar** `t ∈ [0,1]`, moving toward 1 at `1/t_operate` above pull-in, toward 0 at `1/t_release` below drop-out, and **not moving** inside the bi-stable band.
rulings.ruling: Qualify the freeze. Replace '**not moving** inside the bi-stable band' with: 'inside the bi-stable band, an armature already at a stop stays there (t = 0 holds at 0, t = 1 holds at 1); an armature strictly between the stops is *not* in equilibrium and continues in its current direction of travel until it reaches a stop.' Cite BK7 printed p.6 for the reason.
rulings.evidence: BK7 printed p.6 (PDF 11), read on the page image, gives SDC's own mechanism: 'the greater the magnetic force the more likely that the arm will pull in… For a given gap, the greater the voltage the greater the magnetic force; for a given voltage, the smaller the gap, the greater the magnetic force. Since the gap on a closed relay is very small, less voltage is required to hold it in than is required to pull it in.' The band exists *because* force varies with gap — which means it is a property of the two end positions, not of intermediate ones. A literal freeze at, say, t = 0.4 parks the arm inside the both-open window indefinitely, an outcome the mechanism cannot produce and which would deadlock any circuit whose coil voltage lands in the band mid-stroke (exactly the Book VII bias case the model exists to express).
rulings.tag_change: none — the bullet is already [unverified]; the correction is to the physics, not the tag

rulings.currentText: §7.3: 'Note: the component at the top of the POWER strip **varies between surviving units** — one photographed unit carries a red pilot jewel there, another carries a black bayonet FUSEHOLDER cap engraved FUSE. No manual mentions a fuse and the parts list has none. Record as a per-unit variant. `[verified]`'  §12: '| What the factory fitted at the top of the POWER strip (pilot jewel vs fuseholder) | Model the red power light per BK1 p.3; record the fuseholder as a per-unit variant | Panel photographs of several units with known dates |'
rulings.ruling: Close the question against 'per-unit variant'. Rewrite the §7.3 note as: 'The POWER strip runs, top to bottom: power light, the silkscreen legend CIRCUIT BREAKER, the red circuit-breaker pushbutton, then the ON/OFF power switch. Both photographed 601s carry an identical red breaker button under that legend. The top position is the power-light position: the Centre for Computing History unit has a red pilot jewel there, the Commons unit has a black bayonet cap engraved FUSE in the same hole. Factory fit is the light assembly; the fuseholder is an owner replacement of a burnt-out power light. `[verified]`' Delete the §12 row, or restate it as closed.
rulings.evidence: Three independent legs, all read this pass. (1) commons-minivac601-DSCF1392.jpg at native resolution: the POWER strip shows a small red translucent pilot jewel at the top, the two-line silkscreen CIRCUIT BREAKER below it, then a large red pushbutton, then the ON/OFF slide — the exact layout BK1 printed p.3 describes ('The red button above the power switch labeled CIRCUIT BREAKER is a safety switch… The red power light shows when the power is ON'). (2) commons-minivac601-main.jpg at native resolution: the same CIRCUIT BREAKER legend and the same red breaker button are present; only the top item differs, a black cap engraved FUSE / FUSE / FUSE with turn arrows. So the breaker is not the varying part. (3) MAINT printed p.3 (PDF 5) at 600 dpi draws a POWER LIGHT across the + and - output and no fuse anywhere; MAINT printed p.11 lists 6435 Light Assembly and no fuse; a grep for 'fuse' across all six OCR extracts returns only BK1 p.3's simile 'blow just like a household fuse'. This is also the disposition raw/critic-completeness.json C6 prescribes and which components.md did not apply.
rulings.tag_change: the observation stays [verified]; the interpretation moves from 'per-unit variant' to 'owner retrofit into the power-light position'

rulings.section: §8.1, 'Degenerate cases' paragraph; and §1.6, 'Global reset is a power cycle'
rulings.currentText: §8.1: 'Power-on state is every relay OFF (justified by the errata's power-cycle reset).'  §1.6: 'The machine has no reset line; power-on state is every relay de-energised. `[verified]`'
rulings.ruling: Restate as an initial condition, not a settled state. §8.1: 'At power-on every armature *initialises* de-energised (t = 0); the first network solve then runs normally and may immediately pull some relays in. Do not clamp relays OFF after the solve.' §1.6: keep the errata power-cycle sentence, and add 'i.e. the armatures start de-energised — with a Book VII bias resistor fitted, whether a relay is still off after the first solve is exactly what BK7 p.9 step 1 makes the owner test.'
rulings.evidence: The file contradicts itself. §8.2 AT-04 states '120 Ω and below pull in at power-on'. BK7 printed p.9 (PDF 14), read on the page image, makes the whole acceptance criterion for a bias resistor 'Turn power on. If the relay remains OFF (the light will remain off), place a check in the RELAY OFF column' — a test that is only meaningful because a too-small bias resistor makes the relay come on at power-on. An implementer who reads §8.1 literally and forces every relay OFF after the first solve silently destroys the Book VII bias search and AT-04 with it.
rulings.tag_change: §1.6's `[verified]` should attach to the errata power-cycle instruction only, not to the modelling rule

rulings.section: §1.1, paragraph beginning 'The relay unit itself has **eight** solder connections'
rulings.currentText: "That C is *not* one of the relay's eight lugs — i.e. the lamp is a separate part — is a two-source inference: BK1 p.12 says the relay's panel terminals are \"G, H, J, & K, L, N\", and the parts list carries Light Assembly (6435) separately from Relay (6437). `[likely]`"
rulings.ruling: Add the sentence that states it nearly outright and upgrade the tag. Replace the sentence with: 'C is *not* one of the relay's eight lugs — the lamp is a separate part. BK1 printed p.14: *"Three terminals are located directly above each relay on the computer panel. These terminals are connected under the panel to the relay coil. Two terminals are connected directly to the relay coil, and the third terminal is connected to a light wired in series with the relay coil as shown."* Two of C/E/F go to the coil and one goes to the lamp; the Relay Check figure draws exactly six contact terminals plus a two-ended coil, which is MAINT p.8's eight, leaving no lug for C. The parts list carries Light Assembly (6435) separately from Relay (6437) and replaces a lamp by cutting its leads ¾ inch from the terminal, not by unsoldering a relay lug. `[verified]` by deduction.'
rulings.evidence: BK1 printed p.14 (PDF 16), text extracted this pass — the file already quotes the *next* paragraph of that page (the C-and-F vs E-and-F lesson) but not this one. MAINT printed p.8 (PDF 10): 'disconnect the eight connections to the relay'. MAINT printed p.7 (PDF 9), Relay Check figure traced at 600 dpi: H, J, G, L, N, K plus a coil drawn with exactly two ends E and F = eight. MAINT printed p.6 (PDF 8): lamp replacement is 'cut the leads ¾ inch from the terminal'.
rulings.tag_change: `[likely]` → `[verified]` (by deduction, in the same style §1.3 already uses)

An implementation that lights the indicator whenever the coil is energised fails all three.'

confirmedCorrect: MAINT printed→PDF offset (+2) and every single MAINT citation in the file: pp.1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 all re-derived folio by folio and all correct.

§7.1 published-numbers table is complete and exact against MAINT printed p.2/p.3: 110 V AC in, nominal 12 V DC, ~13 V unloaded (p.3 step 3), 1.5 A continuous, all switches 3 A, relay contacts 'in excess of 3 amps', 'lights are operated at less than their rated voltage', 'drive motor is operated at less than one-third rated voltage'. No published electrical figure was missed.

§7.2 power-supply topology, re-traced on a 600 dpi render of MAINT printed p.3: cord → power switch in one black primary leg → transformer primary; centre-tapped secondary with two yellow/black ends into two diodes inside one RECTIFIER block to +; yellow centre tap → CIRCUIT BREAKER → −; POWER LIGHT across + and − downstream of the breaker. Drawn exactly as the file describes.

No filter capacitor and no fuse appear anywhere in the power-supply schematic; the file's [likely] on 'no filter in the chassis' and its explicit refusal to treat absence-from-a-troubleshooting-drawing as conclusive are both the right call.

The two topology consequences: breaker in the DC return carrying total current, and a trip extinguishing the POWER light. MAINT printed p.4 step 9 does name the breaker's terminals as 'the terminal which leads to the transformer' and 'the terminal which leads to the power light'.

§1.4 lamp-in-series topology C–[LAMP]–E–[COIL]–F. BK1 printed p.14's C-and-F vs E-and-F quotation is verbatim-correct, and the panel silkscreen brackets ⌐LIGHT¬ spanning C–E and ⌐COIL¬ spanning E–F are legible at native resolution on commons-minivac601-main.jpg.

MM-RELAY-CHECK fixture: every wire traced on a 600 dpi render of MAINT printed p.7. +/H, +/L, +/Y, X/E, F/−, J/1A, 1B/1−, G/2A, 2B/2−, N/3A, 3B/3−, K/4A, 4B/4− is correct, and C and Z really are drawn as unconnected terminal dots. The relay is drawn OFF with both arms on the N.C. contacts, which is why lights 1 and 3 come on.

The 'eight solder connections = six contact terminals + a two-ended coil' reading, and 'solid = conductor, dashed = mechanical linkage' — the dashed vertical through J/G/N/K is unmistakable at 600 dpi.

§1.5 hysteresis, every element checked against the page images: the pull-in/drop-out definitions and the 'deliberately designed so that there is a great difference' sentence are on BK7 printed p.6 (not p.7, as the §11 correction already records); the two graphs, the shaded region and its 'RELAY WILL REMAIN EITHER ON OR OFF IN THIS REGION' callout are on p.7; both graphs' axes are entirely unnumbered; the second graph adds BIAS VOLTAGE strictly between drop-out and pull-in; and pull-in is drawn strictly inside the span to full supply voltage, so 0 < drop-out < bias < pull-in < full supply holds.
SDC's gap-based physical explanation is quoted correctly from BK7 p.6, and the file is right that it is a better modelling basis than any invented number.

§1.5 bias procedure: 'THE FOLLOWING INSTRUCTIONS ARE FOR A SINGLE RELAY. THIS PROCEDURE MUST BE CARRIED OUT FOR EACH INDIVIDUAL RELAY.' (p.8), the blank Ω_B1…Ω_B6 chart and the 'more than one value' note (p.9), and the descending search for the lowest resistance at which the relay is both off at power-on and on after a momentary press — all confirmed. The file's characterisation of this as primary evidence of unit-to-unit variation is correct and is the right justification for a per-relay spread.

The bias program A/G, B/−, E/X, F/−, H/+, Y/+ plus the braced (+/Ω, Ω/E) is verbatim, and the footnote 'Decreasing values of resistance will be tried here. Start with the highest valued resistor in the kit' is legible on the page image while a grep for 'kit' over book7-capacitor-resistor.txt returns nothing — the file's claim about the OCR layer is exactly right.
The Book VII 601/6010 scope flag is applied uniformly to every BK7 claim, which is the ruling raw/critic-completeness.json C10 demanded and which no other file in the package makes as cleanly.

§6 capacitor facts against BK7 printed pp.10–11: 500 µF for sections 1–5 and 1000 µF for section 6; the 'permanently connected to the negative power source' wiring note; the Ω220 notation example meaning a 220 Ω resistor between 1cap and 1+; the pull-in/drop-out-by-capacitor purpose paragraph; and 'voltage rating not given, only the warning that exceeding it destroys the capacitor'. All quotations accurate.

§1.4's two published lamp-bypass fixes are both real and quoted correctly: ERRATA Book IV p.72 ('the capabilities of the relays are somewhat strained… by-passes the relay indicator lights so that full voltage is supplied to the relay coils') and ERRATA Book V p.11 (remove 5F/6C, 6C/6−; add 5F/6E, 6E/6−, 4E/6C).

§11's errata correction list (BK1 p.13 delete the 1B–2B line; BK1 p.24 diagram label 6Y→6V with the program unaffected; BK2 p.10 DOWN→ON; BK2 p.11 1A/1C→1A/1G; BK2 p.14 2Z/2C→2X/2C; BK4 p.43 2+/2H→1G/2H) matches the errata sheet item for item.

§1.6's Book I Experiment 9 program and BK1 printed p.12's relay text — including the RELAY ON trap sentence 'The two arms (H & L) are connected together. Both contacts always close together.' and the N.O./ARM/N.C. mapping — are verbatim off the page. BK1 printed p.13 is indeed Experiment 6, MANUAL RELAY OPERATION.
